title: Case Report: Longitudinal clonal evolution in EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinoma with coexisting MET exon 14 skipping and EML4-ALK fusion and subsequent KRAS/BRAF bypass mutations.
authors: He Y, Huang W, Xu M et al.
abstract: Acquired resistance to osimertinib in epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-mutant non-small cell lung cancer occurs through on-target mutations or bypass activation of alternative pathways. The longitudinal molecular evolution of a tumor across successive lines of therapy is rarely captured by repeat biopsy. We report a 68-year-old never-smoking woman with EGFR exon 19 deletion lung adenocarcinoma. First-line therapy achieved a partial response, with progression after 10.7 months; after 61 months of osimertinib, re-biopsy revealed concurrent EGFR T790M (9.3%), EML4-ALK fusion (E6:A20; 6.0%), and MET exon 14 skipping (c.3028G>T; 4.0%); aumolertinib plus ensartinib achieved stable disease for approximately 13 months. On further progression, a third biopsy showed molecular changes consistent with clonal evolution: the EML4-ALK fusion, MET exon 14 alteration, and EGFR T790M were no longer detected; the EGFR exon 19 deletion expanded to 47.71%; and KRAS G12R (10.17%), KRAS L19F (7.85%), BRAF D594N (8.13%), and BRAF E501K (6.38%) had emerged. Treatment with ivonescimab, a programmed cell death protein 1 and vascular endothelial growth factor bispecific antibody, plus pemetrexed and carboplatin, followed by pemetrexed plus ivonescimab, achieved stable disease; because chemotherapy was given concurrently, the contribution of ivonescimab cannot be isolated. PD-L1 (tumor proportion score <1%) was assessed on an earlier biopsy and blood tumor mutational burden was measured in 2019. This case is consistent with longitudinal clonal dynamics under sequential targeted therapy, namely regression of drug-sensitive clones and emergence of mitogen-activated protein kinase pathway bypass alterations, and the feasibility of an immunotherapy-containing regimen in a multi-driver tumor with unfavorable immune biomarkers.

title: Case Report: Long-term survival of a patient with lung adenocarcinoma harboring EGFR 19del/T790M/C797S and KIF26B-NTRK1 rearrangement.
authors: Li Z, Liu R, Wu J et al.
abstract: Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) gene mutation stands as one of the most prevalent driver genetic alterations in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). While targeted therapies against EGFR have substantially enhanced patient prognosis, acquired resistance remains a core challenge that limits therapeutic efficacy. Patients with stage IV NSCLC generally exhibit a dismal prognosis, with only about 7% of those with stage IVB disease surviving beyond five years. Herein, we report a case of a 47-year-old female patient diagnosed with advanced lung adenocarcinoma, whose clinical course has persisted for nearly a decade. Initial genetic testing identified an EGFR exon 19 deletion (19del). Following treatment with osimertinib, the patient developed concurrent cis-arranged EGFR T790M/C797S double mutations and a neurotrophic receptor tyrosine kinase 1 (NTRK1) gene rearrangement. Subsequently, through a multimodal therapeutic strategy integrating local intervention, radiation therapy, and targeted therapy, the patient's disease has been sustainably controlled for several years, and she remains alive with stable clinical status to date. NTRK1 fusions are a well-defined mechanism of acquired resistance to EGFR-TKIs, but they are uncommon. This case reports a KIF26B-NTRK1 rearrangement not previously described in lung cancer; however, its functional significance remains to be confirmed. The principal value of this report lies in the completeness of the longitudinal molecular and clinical record, which documents how an on-target mutation and a bypass rearrangement can coexist and persist.

title: Nivolumab Plus Ipilimumab as First-Line Treatment for Patients With Metastatic Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer: Final, 7.5-Year Outcomes From CheckMate 227.
authors: Reck M, Ciuleanu TE, Pluzanski A et al.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: The phase 3 CheckMate 227 Part 1 study (NCT02477826) demonstrated survival benefit with first-line nivolumab plus ipilimumab versus chemotherapy in patients with metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Here, we report final, 7.5-year efficacy and safety results.
METHODS: Adults with stage IV/recurrent NSCLC and no sensitizing EGFR/ALK mutations were stratified by programmed death ligand 1 (PD-L1) ≥1% (n = 1189) or <1% (n = 550) and randomized to nivolumab plus ipilimumab, nivolumab alone (PD-L1 ≥1% only), nivolumab plus chemotherapy (PD-L1 <1% only), or chemotherapy alone. Assessments included overall survival (OS), duration of response, and safety.
RESULTS: At a minimum follow-up of 91.9 months, nivolumab plus ipilimumab continued to demonstrate long-term OS benefit versus chemotherapy in patients with tumor PD-L1 ≥1% (7-year OS rates, 19% versus 10%; hazard ratio [HR], 0.78; 95% CI: 0.67-0.91) or tumor PD-L1 <1% (7-year OS rates, 14% versus 4%; HR, 0.64; 95% CI: 0.51-0.79). Rates of ongoing response at 7 years were higher with nivolumab plus ipilimumab than chemotherapy among responders with tumor PD-L1 ≥1% (25% versus 3%) or tumor PD-L1 <1% (20% versus 3%). Clinical benefit with nivolumab plus ipilimumab was observed across most patient subgroups, including those with squamous or non-squamous NSCLC or selected oncogenic driver mutations. No new safety signals were observed.
CONCLUSIONS: This final analysis from CheckMate 227 confirms that nivolumab plus ipilimumab confers long-term, durable clinical benefit versus chemotherapy in patients with metastatic NSCLC across both the tumor PD-L1 ≥1% and PD-L1 <1% populations, reinforcing nivolumab plus ipilimumab as a first-line treatment option for these patients.

title: Management of Advanced EGFR-Mutant Non-Small-Cell Lung Cancer Across the Disease Course.
authors: Park GH, Kim H, Joe C et al.
abstract: Advances in targeted therapy have improved outcomes for patients with advanced epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-mutant non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Third-generation EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors and first-line combination regimens have expanded treatment options, making the balance between survival benefit, toxicity, treatment burden, and individual patient fitness increasingly important in initial treatment selection. As acquired resistance continues to limit the duration of benefit, this decision must also be considered in the context of subsequent care. At progression, tissue and plasma profiling provide complementary information that can help characterize the diverse mechanisms of resistance and guide further treatment. As resistance-directed therapies and antibody-drug conjugates expand the available treatment options, their selection requires consideration of prior therapy and the pattern of progression, together with molecular findings where relevant. This review examines these interconnected decisions across the course of advanced EGFR-mutant NSCLC, from first-line treatment selection to the assessment and management of acquired resistance. We also address central nervous system involvement, uncommon EGFR mutations, and exon 20 insertions as distinct clinical settings in which disease distribution and the underlying molecular alteration shape treatment choices. By integrating clinical and translational evidence, we discuss how these factors may inform treatment sequencing and individualized care, with attention to survival, quality of life, and the cumulative burden of therapy across the disease course.

title: Real-World Clinical Characteristics and Treatment Patterns of Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor-Mutant Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer: A Nationwide Korean EGFR Registry.
authors: Choi MG, Yeo CD, Yoon SH et al.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Despite advances in epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-targeted therapy for non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), real-world data on diagnostic and treatment patterns across all disease stages remain limited. This study used the nationwide Korean EGFR Registry to characterize contemporary clinical practice in EGFR-mutant NSCLC.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: A total of 1,522 patients with pathologically confirmed EGFR-mutant NSCLC were prospectively enrolled from 40 Korean institutions (June 2022-June 2024). Data on baseline clinical and molecular characteristics, biomarker testing patterns, and treatment for all lines of therapy were collected using standardized electronic case report forms.
RESULTS: The median age of the study population was 68 years, 59.7% were female, and 64.5% were never-smokers. Stage IV disease accounted for 57.8% of cases. The predominant EGFR mutations were exon 19 deletion (48.6%) and L858R (47.1%). NGS was performed for ~23% of patients. In patients with stage IV disease, third-generation TKI use increased markedly (14.3% in 2022 vs. 91.1% in 2024). Stage III management was notably heterogeneous; definitive concurrent chemoradiotherapy was used in only 15.3% of stage III patients overall, with surgery-based treatment predominating in stage IIIA and systemic therapy accounting for all treatment in stage IIIC. The 3-year overall survival rates were 97.2%, 90.9%, 78.3%, and 58.4% for stages I-IV, respectively.
CONCLUSION: This nationwide registry analysis reveals rapid adoption of third-generation TKIs in metastatic EGFR-mutant NSCLC and substantial heterogeneity in stage III disease management. These findings provide clinically meaningful insights into the evolving treatment paradigm of EGFR-mutant NSCLC across disease stages in routine practice.

title: A Study of Glumetinib in Combination With Osimertinib as 1st Line Treatment in Patients With Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer
summary: To evaluate the efficacy and safety of Glumetinib plus Osimertinib in patients with non-small cell lung cancer with classic EGFR mutations and MET overexpression or amplification.

title: Alectinib as Neoadjuvant Treatment in Potentially Resectable Stage III Anaplastic Lymphoma Kinase-Positive Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer: ALNEO Phase II Trial (GOIRC-01-2020-ML42316).
authors: Leonetti A, Boni L, Gnetti L et al.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Stage III non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is a heterogeneous disease with no single definitive therapeutic approach. The role of neoadjuvant tyrosine kinase inhibitors in stage III ALK-positive NSCLC remains unknown. The ALNEO study evaluated the activity and safety of perioperative alectinib in this population.
PATIENTS AND METHODS: ALNEO is an open-label, single-arm, multicenter phase II study enrolling treatment-naïve patients with potentially resectable stage III ALK-positive NSCLC. Patients received neoadjuvant alectinib 600 mg twice daily for 8 weeks, followed by surgery and adjuvant alectinib for up to 96 weeks. The primary end point was major pathologic response (MPR; ≤10% residual viable tumor cells) assessed by blinded independent central review. Secondary end points included pathologic complete response (pCR), objective response rate (ORR), event-free survival (EFS), disease-free survival (DFS), overall survival (OS), and safety.
RESULTS: From May 2021 to July 2024, 33 patients were enrolled. The median age was 62 years (range, 33-79), 70% were female, and 52% were never smokers. Clinical stage was IIIA in 64% and IIIB in 36%. All patients completed neoadjuvant treatment, and 28 (85%) underwent surgery, most commonly lobectomy (75%). R0 resection was achieved in 24 (86%). MPR was observed in 14 patients (42%; 95% CI, 26 to 61), including four pCRs (12%; 95% CI, 3 to 28). ORR was 67%. Adjuvant treatment was initiated in 26 (79%) patients. After a median follow-up of 26.8 months, median EFS, DFS, and OS were not reached; six patients (18%) experienced disease recurrence. Grade ≥3 adverse events occurred in 9% and 27% of patients during neoadjuvant and adjuvant treatment, respectively.
CONCLUSION: The ALNEO study met its primary end point, suggesting perioperative alectinib as a feasible and active approach in potentially resectable stage III ALK-positive NSCLC.

title: Integration of a severe immune-related adverse events predictive model with efficacy biomarkers enables precise stratification in NSCLC immunotherapy: insights from the phase 3 ORIENT-11 study.
authors: Peng Y, Wen L, Shen J et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Severe immune-related adverse events (irAEs) compromise the outcomes of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). However, in routine practice, clinicians still lack biomarkers that can prospectively disentangle antitumor efficacy from the risk of severe irAEs, resulting in largely empirical, one-size-fits-all use of ICIs.
METHODS: In this post hoc analysis of the randomized phase III ORIENT-11 trial, we analyzed RNA-sequencing data from baseline tumor samples of patients with advanced NSCLC receiving Sintilimab (an anti-PD-1 antibody) plus chemotherapy. GSEA and pathway enrichment analyses were performed to elucidate mechanisms of severe irAEs. A predictive model was constructed via 50-time LASSO regressions based on the enriched pathway and was subsequently combined with established efficacy biomarkers (PD-L1 expression and tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte [TIL]) to create a four-quadrant risk-benefit stratification system.
RESULTS: Among 266 patients from the ORIENT-11 trial receiving combination therapy, severe irAEs occurred in 19 (7.14%). The Th17 cell differentiation pathway was significantly enriched in patients with severe irAEs. A predictive model derived from this pathway demonstrated AUC of 0.904 and 0.769 in training and validation cohort, respectively. Due to its independence of efficacy, integration of this toxicity model with PD-L1/TIL-defined efficacy biomarkers stratified patients into four groups, which exhibited differences in ORR (92.9% to 51.1%), severe irAE incidence (0% to 46.7%) and PFS.
CONCLUSIONS: The Th17 differentiation pathway is associated with severe irAEs for NSCLC patients. By integrating a Th17-based severe irAE prediction model with efficacy biomarkers, we propose a four-quadrant risk-benefit stratification framework that supports individualized immunotherapy decisions and moves beyond a one-size-fits-all approach.

title: Incidence and Risk Factors of Postoperative Delirium in Patients with Lung Cancer: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
authors: Quan Q, Jiang H, Zhao Z et al.
abstract: Postoperative delirium (POD) is a frequent neurological complication after lung cancer surgery and is associated with delayed recovery, cognitive decline, prolonged hospitalization, and increased mortality. However, its incidence and risk factors remain inconsistent across studies. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to estimate the pooled cumulative incidence of POD and identify associated risk factors in patients undergoing lung cancer surgery. Nine databases were searched from inception to August 12, 2025, following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) checklist. Eleven studies involving 5,575 patients were included. The pooled cumulative incidence of POD was 12% (95% confidence interval (CI): [0.08, 0.16]), with substantial heterogeneity (I2 = 96.3%, P < 0.001). Subgroup analyses identified significant variation in cumulative incidence across countries, whereas differences by diagnostic tool and surgical type were less conclusive. The incidence was higher in studies from China than in those from Japan, and heterogeneity disappeared in the thoracoscopic radical-resection subgroup. Leave-one-out sensitivity analysis showed that the pooled cumulative incidence remained stable, ranging from 10% to 13%. Significant risk factors included thoracotomy, age ≥75 years, higher American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) classification, prolonged one-lung ventilation, history of coronary heart disease, and history of sedative medication use. Compared with PaO₂ ≤ 60 mmHg, PaO₂ levels of 60 < PaO₂ ≤ 80 mmHg and 80 < PaO₂ ≤ 100 mmHg were associated with lower odds of POD. POD occurs in approximately one in ten patients after lung cancer surgery, highlighting the need for early identification and targeted perioperative prevention.

title: Effect of the timing and setting of pulmonary rehabilitation on functional recovery after lung cancer surgery: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
authors: Zhang W, Zhou Y, Wang W et al.
abstract: ObjectiveTo compare the effects of pulmonary rehabilitation initiated at different times and settings on functional recovery after lung cancer surgery, and to compare supervision modes in late-phase rehabilitation.MethodsPubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, CNKI, CBM and Wanfang Data were searched from inception to October 2026 for randomised controlled trials comparing pulmonary rehabilitation with usual care. Two reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data and assessed bias (RoB 2). Meta-analysis (RevMan 5.4) included sub-group analyses by timing (early in-hospital vs. late out-of-hospital) and supervision mode (fully vs. partially supervised).ResultsThirteen randomised controlled trials (1137 patients) were included. The primary outcomes were post-operative complications and length of hospital stay for early in-hospital rehabilitation, and 6-min walk distance (6MWD), peak oxygen uptake (VO2peak), forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV1) and quality of life (EORTC QLQ-C30) for late-phase rehabilitation. Early rehabilitation did not significantly reduce complications (risk ratio = 0.55, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.25-1.24) or shorten hospital stay (mean difference = -0.08 days, 95% CI -1.19 to 1.04). Late rehabilitation significantly improved 6MWD (mean difference = 68.86 m, 95% CI 53.46-84.26), VO2peak (mean difference = 2.62 ml/kg/min, 95% CI 2.08-3.15) and FEV1 (mean difference = 0.52 L, 95% CI 0.22-0.81), but not quality of life. Fully and partially supervised modes did not differ significantly in 6MWD.ConclusionLate rehabilitation improved exercise capacity and pulmonary function after lung cancer surgery, whereas early in-hospital rehabilitation did not show clear short-term benefits. Partially supervised models may offer a feasible alternative to fully supervised rehabilitation. Staged, individualised pulmonary rehabilitation warrants further investigation.

title: Lung cancer screening in the European Union - the size and characteristics of the eligible population.
authors: Bartekova K, de Nijs K, Heijnsdijk EAM et al.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Feasibility evaluation of lung cancer screening (LCS) using low-dose computed tomography for high-risk individuals has been recommended in the EU. Unlike other cancer screening programs, LCS eligibility depends on the individuals' smoking history. However, the size, health status, and screening behavior of the eligible population across the EU remain poorly characterized.
METHODS: We used the European Health Interview Survey (EHIS)(wave 3, collected mostly in 2019) to estimate the number of individuals aged 50-80 eligible for LCS in the EU under two criteria: the United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) 2021 guidelines and the risk-based PLCOm2012 model (six-year-risk≥1.51%). We assessed health status and adherence to established cancer-screening programs (colorectal, breast, cervical) of LCS-eligibles using mixed-effects regression.
RESULTS: An estimated 25.38million individuals(16.16% of 50-80-year-olds) met the USPSTF2021 criteria in 2019, while 16.42million(10.45%) were eligible under risk-based criteria, with substantial inter-country-variation. Screening-eligibles reported poorer health, including higher prevalence of chronic respiratory and cardiovascular conditions. They also showed 24-29% lower adherence to existing cancer screening programs.
CONCLUSIONS: Our findings highlight the need for country-specific LCS strategies that consider both eligibility criteria and healthcare capacity. More intensive and targeted strategies to encourage participation will be essential.

title: A single-arm, phase II study of ivonescimab in combination with FOLFOX in advanced HER2 negative gastroesophageal adenocarcinomas.
authors: Durbin SM, Strickland MR, Sahin I et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Gastroesophageal adenocarcinoma (GEA) is a major cause of global cancer-related deaths. A first-line standard of care for advanced GEA is FOLFOX, with the addition of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) in patients with a programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) combined positive score of ≥1. However, overall survival remains poor. There is a strong mechanistic rationale for cooperativity between anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) antibodies and ICIs across cancers. Ivonescimab is a bispecific antibody that simultaneously targets programmed cell death protein 1 and VEGF, with evidence of safety and efficacy in colorectal, hepatocellular, and lung cancers.
DESIGN: This single-arm, multi-institutional, phase II study seeks to evaluate ivonescimab in combination with FOLFOX as a first-line therapy in GEA. Adults with locally advanced unresectable or metastatic human epidermal growth factor 2 (HER2)-negative GEA are eligible. Positive PD-L1 expression is not required for eligibility. We plan to enroll 40 patients. Ivonescimab 20 mg/kg and FOLFOX are given on day 1 and day 15 of a 28-day cycle. Treatment will continue until disease progression, withdrawal of consent, or death. The primary objective is to define the efficacy of ivonescimab in combination with FOLFOX as measured by the 6-month progression-free survival rate. Translational correlative studies are planned to explore tumor and immunologic determinants of response.

title: Cancer risk and survival outcomes in germline POT1 variant carriers.
authors: Raper AC, Schultz BI, Kim J et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The prevalence of germline POT1 variants, spectrum of associated tumors, cancer risk and survival outcomes are incompletely described, and clinical management guidelines vary. We evaluated POT1 variant carriers in three biobanks and a clinical cohort to address these limitations.
METHODS: Prevalence, cancer spectrum and risk associated with germline POT1 pathogenic/likely pathogenic and additional functionally assessed variants were evaluated in Penn Medicine Biobank (PMBB; n =51,172), Geisinger MyCode (MyCode; n =220,582), UK Biobank (UKBB; n =469,558) and a Penn Medicine clinical cohort.
RESULTS: Estimated POT1 variant prevalence ranged from 1:1,279 to 1:2,902. Compared to non-carriers, cancer diagnoses were more frequent among POT1 variant carriers in PMBB (OR 3.41, 95%CI 1.81-6.43, p =1.88x10 -4 ), MyCode (OR 2.23, 95%CI 1.31-3.79, p=0.003), and UKBB (OR 1.40, 95%CI 1.07-1.84, p =0.015). Cancer incidence increased beginning in the mid-30s, without evidence of increased mortality. Along with previously described cancer types, lung cancer was associated with POT1 variant carriers in two biobank cohorts.
CONCLUSION: POT1 is a cancer susceptibility gene associated with a moderate (1.5-3.5-fold) increased cancer risk. Variants are relatively frequent and predispose to a broad tumor spectrum and increased incidence starting in the mid-30s, without increasing mortality. These findings expand understanding of POT1 -associated disease and provide data to inform clinical management.

title: Lorlatinib-Associated Dyslipidemia in ALK-Positive NSCLC: Atherosclerotic Risk and the Unresolved Question of Venous Thromboembolism.
authors: Srirangadhamu Gopu S, Hasan Shadali Abdul Khader A, Patel AP et al.
abstract: Lorlatinib, a brain-penetrant third-generation anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) tyrosine kinase inhibitor, has markedly improved outcomes in ALK-positive non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). In the CROWN trial, median progression-free survival had not been reached with first-line lorlatinib after 7 years of follow-up, compared with 9.1 months for crizotinib, with 7-year progression-free survival of 55% versus 3%. Median treatment duration was 62.6 months versus 9.6 months. This duration extends cumulative exposure to lorlatinib's characteristic metabolic toxicity: hypercholesterolemia and hypertriglyceridemia. At 7 years, these occurred in 73% and 71% of patients receiving lorlatinib, with grade 3 or 4 events in 22% and 26%. Onset is rapid, at a median of about 2 weeks. At 5 years, any-grade elevations had persisted for a median of 36 to 38 months; 71% of events were managed with lipid-lowering agents. ALK-positive NSCLC carries a high risk of venous thromboembolism across observational cohorts and a meta-analysis, more so for venous than arterial events. Laboratory evidence suggests the EML4-ALK fusion raises tissue factor through the pERK1/2-AP-1 pathway. At 7 years, aggregate cardiovascular adverse events were similar between treatment groups, and venous events were not more frequent with lorlatinib; small event counts and differing treatment exposure limit comparison of individual events. Statin choice is limited because lorlatinib is a moderate cytochrome P450 3A inducer; rosuvastatin and pravastatin are preferred. We review lorlatinib-associated dyslipidemia and its management and separate two claims: prompt, guideline-concordant lipid management is supported by established atherosclerotic prevention principles, whereas any effect on venous thromboembolism remains untested.

title: ERS clinical practice guidelines for the management of patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and lung cancer.
authors: Tzouvelekis A, Hellemons ME, Billiet C et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Managing patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) and concomitant lung cancer is a major clinical challenge due to increased incidence and negative impact on quality of life and mortality. Evidence-based recommendations are lacking. This European Respiratory Society (ERS) clinical practice guideline provides recommendations to balance oncological benefits against treatment-associated toxicity.
METHODS: An ERS multidisciplinary Task Force of experts and patient representatives produced 11 conditional recommendations across seven PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome) questions and two narrative questions; for one PICO question no recommendation was issued. Systematic reviews were performed for each question. Evidence certainty was assessed using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluation) approach (for PICOs) and recommendations were formulated using the Evidence-to-Decision framework.
RESULTS: For early-stage lung cancer, the Task Force suggests surgical resection in medically fit patients. Postoperative risk necessitates systematic preoperative evaluation, perioperative antifibrotic therapy discussion and protective perioperative strategies. For stereotactic radiotherapy, a conditional recommendation for either the intervention or the comparison was issued, balancing potential oncological benefit against radiation pneumonitis. In locally advanced lung cancer, the Task Force suggests not administering concurrent radio-chemotherapy, due to very high acute exacerbation rates. For advanced lung cancer, chemotherapy is suggested in medically fit patients, where survival benefits outweigh increased toxicity risks. For stage IV lung cancer, evidence for immunotherapy was limited, thus a conditional recommendation for either the intervention or the comparison was issued. Evidence for targeted therapy for lung cancer in patients with IPF was insufficient to support a recommendation.
CONCLUSION: Given the poor prognosis of both conditions and treatment-associated risks, management requires multidisciplinary assessment of competing risks and patient preferences in experienced interstitial lung disease and oncology centres.

title: "Patient Experiences During and Beyond Treatment with Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors: A Systematic Review of Qualitative Research and Implications for Gastrointestinal Cancer".
authors: Collantes-Espinosa L, Cruickshank S, Muls A
abstract:
METHODS: Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) and Enhancing Transparency in Reporting the Synthesis of Qualitative Research (ENTREQ) guidelines, we systematically searched PubMed, Embase, MEDLINE, Cochrane Library, Global Health, and Journals@Ovid for studies published between January 2014 and January 2025. Eligible studies were qualitative or mixed methods reports of patient experiences with ICIs; studies that did not report primary patient data were excluded. Quality was assessed using the Joanna Briggs Institute checklist for qualitative research, and the data were analyzed thematically.
RESULTS: Thirty studies published between 2017 and 2025 were included, covering melanoma, lung cancer, and mixed solid tumor populations. Analysis identified six overarching themes: (1) prognostic uncertainty and expectations; (2) information needs and decision-making; (3) treatment burden and physical functioning; (4) psychosocial identity and social roles; (5) emotional and existential well-being; and (6) economic and practical impact. Patients generally perceived ICIs as more tolerable than chemotherapy but reported persistent toxicities, uncertainty regarding treatment durability, and psychosocial strain. The perspectives and experiences of caregivers regarding treatment discontinuation were underrepresented. No study specifically examined GI cancers.
CONCLUSIONS: ICIs are experienced as both a lifeline and a burden. The absence of GI cancer perspectives represents a critical research gap in this field. Future studies should prioritize GI cancers, caregivers, long-term survivors, and patients with poor outcomes to inform patient-centered supportive care.
IMPLICATIONS FOR NURSING PRACTICE: This review highlights the need for personalised communication, routine assessment of psychosocial well-being, and proactive management of irAEs in patients receiving immunotherapy. Multidisciplinary supportive care should address the physical, psychological, practical, and financial impact of treatment. Given the limited representation of GI cancers in the current literature, further work is needed to ensure supportive care strategies adequately reflect the needs of this population.
REGISTRATION: PROSPERO CRD42024568112.

title: Novel C-N bond-bridged heterobivalent β-carboline derivatives as lysosome-targeted antitumor agents targeting PPT1: Design, synthesis, biological evaluation, and mechanism of action.
authors: Chen S, Wei J, Yun S et al.
abstract: A series of C-N bond-bridged heterobivalent β-carboline derivatives (11a-11w) was designed by transplanting the dimeric, tri-basic, lysosomotropic architecture of the palmitoyl-protein thioesterase 1 (PPT1) inhibitor DQ661 into a rigidified β-carboline framework, and synthesized via deep-eutectic-solvent-catalyzed reductive amination. Compound 11j (R9' = 4-fluorobenzyl) was the most broadly active member of the series (IC50 = 2.3-7.1 μM against five tumor cell lines, lower than those of cisplatin). In Lewis lung carcinoma (LLC) cells, compound 11j suppressed migration, induced G0/G1 cell-cycle arrest and reduced DNA synthesis, and it disrupted tube formation in human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVEC) and angiogenesis in the chicken chorioallantoic membrane (CAM) assay. Mechanistically, compound 11j accumulated in lysosomes, and lysosomal alkalinization abolished its cytotoxicity; together with the suppressed PI3K/Akt phosphorylation, surface plasmon resonance showing concentration-dependent, structure-selective binding to PPT1 and the direct inhibition of PPT1 thioesterase activity identify the lysosomal depalmitoylase PPT1 as its molecular target. Fpocket-guided consensus docking (FRED/Gnina/Uni-Mol) against monomeric PPT1 converged on four candidate sites, and molecular dynamics simulations identified the orthosteric catalytic groove (G4) as the most probable binding site. In silico absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion and toxicity (ADMET) prediction indicated a drug-like profile for compound 11j, although its high lipophilicity and predicted hERG II liability warrant attention in future optimization. These results suggest compound 11j as a lysosome-targeted PPT1 inhibitor candidate linking organelle-level targeting to anti-angiogenic activity.

title: Timing of Alectinib in Resectable ALK-Positive Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer: Lessons From ALNEO.
authors: Borgeaud M, Mariniello A, Addeo A

title: Aerobic exercise inhibits lung adenocarcinoma invasion dependent on the superior cervical ganglion.
authors: Meng F, Wang T, Cui Y et al.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To elucidate possible neural and molecular pathway mechanisms underlying the suppression of aerobic exercise in lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) invasion.
METHODS: Sympathetic nerve distribution was visualized via immunofluorescent staining in human tissue microarrays (TMAs) and mouse lung specimens. Pseudorabies virus (PRV) retrograde tracing method was employed to identify the brain-lung neural circuit, and superior cervical ganglionectomy was administrated to achieve pulmonary sympathetic denervation. Voluntary wheel running (VWR) worked as an aerobic exercise to intervene the brain-lung neural circuit to suppress mouse LUAD invasion. Norepinephrine (NE) levels and the expression of ADRB2 and MMP2 were assessed using ELISA, Western blot and qRT-PCR methods. RNA sequencing, along with transwell and wound-healing assays, were conducted on lentiviral-mediated ADRB2-overexpressing LUAD cells to evaluate migratory and invasive behaviors.
RESULTS: Substantial sympathetic nerve infiltration was detected in both human and mouse LUAD specimens, with a negative correlation observed between intratumoral sympathetic nerve density and tumor volume. Retrograde tracing revealed that pulmonary sympathetic nerves are predominantly innervated by the superior cervical ganglion (SCG). SCG resection abrogated the exercise-induced elevation in intratumoral NE and reversed the anti-invasion benefits of exercise. In vitro, NE treatment downregulated MMP2 expression and impaired the migration and invasion of LUAD cells. Similarly, ADRB2 overexpression suppresses LUAD invasion by inhibiting MMP2 expression.
CONCLUSION: The SCG acts as a relay hub connecting higher brain centers to intratumoral sympathetic activity, and VWR engages this SCG-mediated pathway to exert an anti-invasive effect on LUAD invasion. VWR stimulates NE release from intratumoral sympathetic nerves in LUAD. NE inhibits LUAD invasion via the ADRB2-MMP2 signaling pathway.

title: Gut microbiome and immunotherapy in advanced non-small cell lung cancer: a prospective cohort study.
authors: Kapoor A, Chaudhary M, Gupta A et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The gut microbiome (GM) is increasingly recognized as a determinant of immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) efficacy in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). However, most available evidence originates from Western, Bacteroides-dominant populations. Understanding GM characteristics in diverse ecological and dietary settings is crucial for global biomarker development.
METHODS: This is a prospective, observational study conducted at a tertiary cancer hospital. 50 adults with advanced NSCLC initiating PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitor-based therapy (with or without chemotherapy) between March 2024 and January 2025 were enrolled. Eligibility required ECOG performance status 0-2 and absence of concurrent antibiotics or probiotics. Paired stool samples were collected at baseline (T0) and first radiologic evaluation (T1, approximately 8-12 weeks). The aim was to characterize baseline and early-on-treatment gut microbiome composition and diversity in Indian patients with advanced NSCLC receiving ICI therapy and to explore associations with clinical outcomes between Responders (CR/PR/SD) vs. Non-Responders (PD).
RESULTS: Among 50 enrolled patients (median age, 56 years; 52% male; 84% adenocarcinoma), 38 were responders and 12 nonresponders. The gut microbiome was Prevotella-dominant (P. copri ≈ 40% relative abundance). No significant differences in α-diversity (Shannon P = .47; Simpson P = .66) or β-diversity (PERMANOVA R²<0.03, P > .2) were observed. Nominal enrichment of Bacteroides sp. AM16 15, Holdemanella biformis, and Phocaeicola salanitronis was seen in responders, whereas Escherichia coli and other Proteobacteria were higher in some non-responders. Akkermansia muciniphila and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii showed no significant association with response.
CONCLUSIONS: This first Indian NSCLC microbiome study establishes a Prevotella-rich regional baseline and underscores that microbiome-immunotherapy associations observed in Western cohorts may not be universal. Population-specific, functionally oriented, multi-omic studies are warranted to guide globally translatable microbiome-based interventions.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: The study was registered with Clinical Trial Registry of India (CTRI, 2024/03/081240) before starting enrolment in the study.

title: Focused Ultrasound Hyperthermia for Spatiotemporal Activation of Engineered Chimeric Antigen Receptor T Cells in a Prostate Cancer Mouse Model.
authors: Wei F, He P, Yoon CW et al.
abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy has demonstrated remarkable clinical success in hematological malignancies but remains limited in solid tumors by on-target off-tumor toxicity and the inability to precisely control therapeutic activity within the tumor microenvironment. This protocol presents a workflow for localized, spatiotemporal activation of engineered CAR T cells using focused ultrasound (FUS)-induced hyperthermia. Engineered T cells containing heat shock promoter (HSP)-regulated gene circuits (EchoBack CAR T cells) remain functionally latent until activated by localized hyperthermia. The protocol describes the generation of a subcutaneous prostate cancer mouse model, local subcutaneous administration of EchoBack chimeric antigen receptor T cells proximal to the tumor, accurate alignment of the focused ultrasound transducer, and localized thermal stimulation. A central feature of the workflow is a focused ultrasound system integrated with a closed-loop proportional-integral-derivative (PID) controller that continuously adjusts acoustic power using real-time intratumoral temperature measurements obtained with a needle thermocouple. This feedback-controlled approach maintains hyperthermia at approximately 43°C for 15 min while limiting temperature fluctuations. Hardware assembly instructions, software code, and experimental procedures are provided to facilitate reproducible implementation. This protocol enables spatially controlled activation of engineered chimeric antigen receptor T cells within tumors and provides bioengineers and immunologists with a practical platform for investigating ultrasound-responsive synthetic biology and controllable cellular immunotherapies in preclinical mouse models.

title: ATMPs in oncology: A comprehensive review of CAR-T and CIK cell therapies within the European regulatory framework.
authors: Callegarin F, De Salvo GL, Rosato A et al.
abstract: Advanced therapy medicinal products (ATMPs), encompassing gene, somatic cell, and tissue-engineered products, represent a paradigm shift in clinical oncology governed by a highly dynamic European Union (EU) regulatory framework. While existing literature often treats clinical biology and pharmaceutical legislation in isolation, this review uniquely bridges the gap by providing a critical, multi-layered evaluation of ATMP cell platforms in the context of Europe's shifting regulatory architecture over the last decade. We analyze the operational impacts of the clinical trials information system (CTIS), the strategic utility of the hospital exemption (HE) pathway for academic innovation, and the newly effective, risk-adapted 2025 European Medicines Agency (EMA) guidelines (EMA/CAT/22473/2025). Clinically, our analysis reveals a clear contrast between two platforms: chimeric antigen receptor T cell (CAR-T) therapies are highly effective in hematological malignancies, but their wider use is restricted by life-threatening toxicities, complex centralized logistics, and solid tumor microenvironment (TME) barriers. In contrast, cytokine-induced killer (CIK) cells offer a safe and cost-effective alternative, demonstrating clinical value when integrated into synergistic combinatorial regimens. Finally, we outline the future outlook of the ATMP landscape, discussing how emerging frontiers will address current financial and clinical bottlenecks, ultimately redefining the scalability and global accessibility of adoptive immunotherapies.

title: CAR-T and CAR-NK cell therapy targets in gastrointestinal malignancies: a narrative review of clinical evidence and future directions.
authors: Ismail M, Al-Gizey N, Al-Najjar E et al.
abstract: Gastrointestinal (GI) malignancies account for more than one-third of cancer-related deaths worldwide, and outcomes for advanced disease remain poor despite advances in systemic therapy and immunotherapy. Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-engineered cellular therapies have transformed the treatment of hematologic malignancies, but their application in solid tumors has been limited by antigen heterogeneity, immunosuppressive tumor microenvironments, on-target/off-tumor toxicity, and manufacturing challenges. This narrative review examines the clinical evidence supporting chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) and chimeric antigen receptor natural killer (CAR-NK) therapies directed against six major targets in GI oncology: claudin 18.2 (CLDN18.2), guanylyl cyclase C (GUCY2C), mesothelin (MSLN), glypican-3 (GPC3), carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), and human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2). Among these, CLDN18.2 is the most advanced target; in the randomized phase II CT041-ST-01 trial, satricabtagene autoleucel significantly improved progression-free survival (PFS) compared with physician's choice therapy in previously treated gastric or gastroesophageal junction cancer, providing the first randomized evidence of CAR-based therapy efficacy in a solid tumor. GUCY2C and GPC3 have shown promising early-phase activity in metastatic colorectal cancer and hepatocellular carcinoma, respectively, whereas mesothelin, CEA, and HER2 continue to face important biological and safety challenges. CAR-NK cells have emerged as a complementary platform with favorable safety characteristics and off-the-shelf manufacturing potential, although clinical experience in GI malignancies remains limited. We discuss the relative clinical maturity of these targets, key barriers to implementation, and emerging strategies that may advance the role of CAR-based cellular therapies in GI cancers.

title: Macrophage state in neoadjuvant and perioperative immunotherapy resistance in resectable NSCLC: a critical appraisal of strategies from CSF1R and CD47-SIRPα to CAR-macrophages.
authors: Li H, Li B, Li Z et al.
abstract: Neoadjuvant or perioperative chemoimmunotherapy has become a standard treatment option for selected patients with resectable non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), with eligibility determined by tumor stage, nodal involvement, oncogenic-driver status, regimen, and jurisdiction. Even so, most patients do not achieve a pathological complete response, and the determinants of resistance in early-stage disease remain incompletely understood. Tumor-associated macrophages are a key, and targetable, component of that resistance. We argue that abundance alone is an insufficient predictor of whether the myeloid compartment supports or suppresses a checkpoint-dependent response, and that macrophage state, namely the dominant subset, its spatial niche, and its trajectory under therapy, adds explanatory and therapeutic information whose weight remains to be established. Single-cell and spatial studies have identified metabolically distinct SPP1+, CCL18+, and oncofetal STAB1+ states associated with immunosuppressive niches in NSCLC, although these labels vary between datasets and their functional assignments are provisional. Limited serial neoadjuvant data from a single cohort suggest that treatment expands tissue-resident macrophages and shifts tumor-associated macrophages toward a neutral rather than antitumor phenotype, most evidently in tumors that reached a major pathological response. Current agents, including CSF1R and CD47-SIRPα blockade, TREM2, LILRB2 and PI3Kγ inhibitors, and chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) macrophages, act on programs that cut across these subsets rather than on the subsets themselves, and almost all efficacy evidence derives from advanced or preclinical disease. The resectable, biomarker-rich perioperative window is nonetheless the most informative setting in which to test subset-informed myeloid reprogramming.

title: Integrative Bioinformatics-Driven Discovery of the Novel Chimeric Antigen Receptor (CAR)-T Cell Targets Erb-B2 Receptor Tyrosine Kinase 3 (ErbB3) and Solute Carrier Family 1 Member 5 (SLC1A5) in Melanoma.
authors: Juraschek KF, Güse E, Hof MMC et al.
abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy has shown limited success in solid tumors, mainly because of the scarcity of tumor-specific surface antigens. To address this challenge, we developed an integrated computational and experimental pipeline for antigen discovery and applied it to melanoma. Our bioinformatics strategy introduced a novel quantitative metric, the restrictiveness ratio, to identify antigens highly expressed in tumors but minimally present in healthy tissues. Using RNA-sequencing data from patient samples, we compared candidate targets with the established melanoma antigen chondroitin sulphate proteoglycan 4 (CSPG4) and validated their expression on melanoma cell lines. CARs were engineered against selected antigens, CAR-T cells were generated by RNA electroporation, and expression was confirmed. Functional validation included T cell activation, cytokine secretion, and cytotoxicity assays. RNA-seq analysis of cutaneous and uveal melanoma identified 90 and 84 candidate genes, respectively, encoding transmembrane proteins with tumor expression above 10 TPM (transcripts per million). Fifty-six genes displayed higher restrictiveness ratios than CSPG4. Following manual curation and scFv (single-chain variable fragment) availability assessment, five candidates were prioritized. CARs targeting ErbB3 and SLC1A5 induced strong antigen-specific T cell activation and cytotoxicity comparable to CSPG4-CARs. These findings identify ErbB3 and SLC1A5 as promising CAR-T targets and establish an integrative bioinformatics-driven framework for extending CAR-T therapy to solid tumors.

title: Targeted cancer ablation via programmable sensing of amplified oncogenic RNA.
authors: Zhang M, Hu Y, Yamada-Hunter SA et al.
abstract: Selectively eliminating cancer cells based on their oncogenic drivers holds great promise but remains challenging for targeted cancer therapy. Here, we present ORCA (Oncogenic RNA-triggered Cancer Ablation), a programmable and modular platform that couples RADAR-based detection of oncogenic RNA with conditional expression of therapeutic payloads in cancer cells. We identify RADAR sensors targeting the transcripts of endogenously amplified oncogenes, including MYC , FGFR2 and wild-type KRAS in colorectal and gastric cancer cells. Focusing on colorectal cancer (CRC) driven by extrachromosomal DNA-amplified MYC , we demonstrate targeted ablation of high- MYC cancer cells using two orthogonal strategies: anti-CD19 CAR-T therapy and enzyme-prodrug therapy. In vivo delivery of ORCA using adeno-associated virus (AAV) suppresses tumor growth in a subcutaneous xenograft model and prolongs survival in a CRC liver metastasis model. ORCA establishes oncogenic RNAs as actionable inputs for targeted cancer therapy via programmable RNA sensing, thus offering a strategy to target tumors through the transcripts of otherwise difficult-to-drug oncogenes such as MYC .

title: A Standalone PD-1 Chimeric Switch Receptor T-Cell Platform Expands the Therapeutic Window of PD-L1 Targeting in Solid Tumors.
authors: Luo Y, Guo S, Qie Y et al.
abstract:
UNLABELLED: Programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) is a promising therapeutic target owing to its broad expression on tumor cells and immunosuppressive myeloid cells within the tumor microenvironment (TME), providing an opportunity to target both cellular compartments. However, physiological PD-L1 expression in normal tissues poses a substantial risk of on-target/off-tumor toxicity, limiting the therapeutic window and clinical translation of PD-L1-targeted cellular therapies. Here, we developed a standalone programmed death-1 (PD-1) chimeric switch receptor (CSR) T-cell platform designed to preserve the therapeutic advantages of PD-L1 targeting while improving tumor-normal discrimination. Iterative receptor engineering, with antitumor activity and normal-cell reactivity evaluated as parallel selection criteria, identified two lead PD-1 CSR T-cell candidates. Compared with our previously developed antibody-based PD-L1 CAR T cells, the lead candidates retained potent PD-L1-specific cytotoxicity against tumor cells while exhibiting markedly reduced cytotoxicity against primary human small airway epithelial cells, astrocytes, renal epithelial cells, hepatocytes, and cardiomyocytes. They also efficiently eliminated PD-L1-positive immunosuppressive myeloid cells and mediated dual-compartment targeting of tumor and myeloid cells in three-dimensional (3D) multicellular tumor organoids. In vivo, both candidates suppressed tumor growth and prolonged survival in orthotopic breast cancer and patient-derived glioblastoma models after systemic and intracranial administration, respectively. Collectively, these findings establish PD-1 CSR T cells as a standalone therapeutic platform that expands the therapeutic window of PD-L1-targeted cellular therapy by preserving dual-compartment targeting of tumor and immunosuppressive myeloid cells while reducing normal-cell reactivity, providing a foundation for further clinical translation across solid tumors.
ONE SENTENCE SUMMARY: A standalone PD-1 CSR T-cell platform improves the safety of PD-L1 targeting while preserving tumor and myeloid cell activity.

title: Current perspectives of CAR-T cells therapy in peritoneal carcinomatosis.
authors: Qian-Zhang S, Domínguez-Prieto V, Romero-Triana D et al.
abstract: Peritoneal carcinomatosis (PC) is a frequent pattern of tumor dissemination across multiple malignancies, including colorectal, gastric, ovarian, and pancreatic cancers, and is associated with poor prognosis and limited survival. Although cytoreductive surgery (CRS) with or without hyperthermic intraperitoneal chemotherapy (HIPEC) has improved outcomes in selected patients, its indication remains restricted, leaving a substantial proportion of patients without curative options, and recurrence rates remain high even after treatment. Therefore, the development of novel therapeutic strategies is urgently needed. Chimeric antigen receptor T (CAR-T) cell therapy has emerged as a promising approach, achieving remarkable success in hematological malignancies and gaining increasing attention in solid tumors. Several tumor-associated antigens, including CEA, CLDN18.2, GUCY2C, EpCAM, and mesothelin, have been investigated across different tumor types, showing encouraging preclinical and early clinical results. In particular, similar to HIPEC, regional delivery strategies such as intraperitoneal administration may enhance tumor targeting, improve cell trafficking, and increase therapeutic efficacy in peritoneal disease. However, CAR-T cell therapy in PC faces important challenges inherent to solid tumors, including antigen heterogeneity, limited tumor trafficking and infiltration, and a hostile tumor microenvironment characterized by dense stromal barriers and immunosuppressive conditions, which ultimately limit its efficacy. Overcoming these barriers is essential to optimize therapeutic outcomes. This review summarizes the current evidence on CAR-T cell therapy in major solid tumors associated with PC, highlighting key targets, administration strategies, and clinical outcomes, while addressing the main limitations and emerging strategies to improve its clinical application, as well as future perspectives for its integration into multimodal treatment approaches.

title: A scalable tumor-vasculature-on-chip for CAR T cell trafficking and efficacy studies.
authors: de Haan L, Olczyk A, Olivier T et al.
abstract: Most cellular therapies, like CAR T cells, remain ineffective in solid tumors. This is primarily due to a complex tumor microenvironment (TME), which creates biochemically hostile and often immunosuppressive conditions that limit efficacy of immunotherapies. Besides, cellular therapy efficacy is still often established in traditional 2D cultures that fail to simulate relevant aspects of solid tumor biology. Recent advances in three-dimensional (3D) and organ-on-chip culture systems have provided more physiologically relevant models for immunotherapy testing. These microphysiological systems (MPS) not only offer a 3D environment that alters tumor cell sensitivity to therapy but also enable inclusion of TME components and assessment of processes such as extravasation and infiltration, key steps in CAR T cell activity in vivo. This study focuses on applying an advanced culture technique and further building on the use of a scalable on-chip platform, the OrganoPlate, to grow EpCAM-positive and EpCAM-negative tumor cells in coculture with an endothelial vessel to study EpCAM-targeting CAR T cell migration and killing kinetics. The CAR T cells specifically targeted and killed EpCAM-positive HT-29 tumor cells while EpCAM-negative A375 tumor cells were not affected. In addition, target cell killing was dependent on the ratio between CAR T and tumor cells (E:T ratio) and was enhanced by addition of IL-2. Inflammatory cytokines like INF-γ, TNFα and IL-6 increased overtime in cultures containing CAR T cells. Morphometric analyses of the endothelial compartment showed E:T ratio dependent disruption of endothelial vessels. Additionally, this system was able to distinguish EpCAM ScFv-CD28-CD3z and EpCAM ScFv-TM-4-1BB-CD3z CAR T cells killing abilities and was used for studying the effect of immune checkpoint inhibitors and Temozolomide, a DNA targeting drug, on CAR T cell performance. Altogether, this work adds to the available advanced culture techniques for immunotherapy developers by describing a model that is modular, scalable, and suitable for phenotypic and functional characterization of CAR T cells.

title: LCatlas: A Point-Of-Care Tool for Predicting Immunotherapy Outcomes in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer
summary: Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remains a leading cause of cancer mortality, with a minority of patients experiencing durable responses to first-line immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). Currently, there are no easily accessible tools to predict clinical benefit to first-line immunotherapy. To address this gap, we developed LCatlas (https://www.lcatlas.org), a point-of-care web application designed to predict immunotherapy outcomes and inform evidence-based treatment decisions. Using data from 79 NSCLC patients receiving first-line immunotherapy, we extracted demographic, clinical, and molecular features from electronic medical records and compared three independent approaches, statistical model (logistic regression), machine learning (XGboost), and AI model (TabTransformer) to identify the most effective predictor. LCatlas accepts nine variables, gender, smoking history, bone/pleura/liver metastasis, PDL1 tumor staining, albumin level, hemoglobin level, lymphocyte count, neutrophil count, and platelet count, to predict responses to both immunotherapy and immunotherapy plus chemotherapy. LCatlas cross-validation yielded an area under the curve (AUC) of 79% [72% - 85%], with sensitivity of 87% [72% - 95%] and specificity of 78% [64% - 89%], outperforming previous studies including high-volume data-driven deep-learning approaches. In a validation cohort consisting of 28 individuals, it demonstrated a prediction accuracy of 82%. LCatlas may serve as a valuable point-of-care tool by identifying patients likely to experience extended immunotherapy or combination therapy using readily available medical data. Its evidence-based approach can optimize personalized treatment planning and thereby promote quality and safety of care.

title: # Treatment- and tissue-context-specific isotope labeling patterns in patient-derived lung cancer tissues: an independent reanalysis of public metabolomics data
summary: Publicly deposited stable-isotope-resolved metabolomics data can be reanalyzed independently, but small patient-derived experiments may produce treatment effects with limited statistical resolution. We reanalyzed a public isotope-resolved metabolomics dataset from patient-derived lung cancer tissue cultures to quantify treatment- and tissue-specific labeling patterns and their uncertainty. We used 38 tissue samples from two patients: matched tumor and non-tumor slices from UK131 treated with vehicle or pembrolizumab and traced with U-13C6-glucose or U-13C5,15N2-glutamine (n = 3 per cell), and a pembrolizumab x WGP {beta}-glucan factorial experiment in UK2035 tumor tissue (n = 3/3/3/2). We recomputed protein-normalized pools, isotopologue distributions, atom-percent excess and pathway summaries. Effects were estimated with log2-scale linear models, Hedges' g, and exact randomization tests that enumerated all assignments compatible with each design; Benjamini-Hochberg q values were calculated within endpoint families. Sixteen macrophage samples were examined only descriptively. In UK131 tumor tissue, labeled non-oxidative pentose phosphate pathway intermediates increased 1.84-fold (model P = 0.036; exact tumor P = 0.10; exact interaction P = 0.16; q = 0.32). Weighted isotopic scrambling increased 1.31-fold (exact interaction P = 0.04; q = 0.20), and glutamine-derived glutathione diversion increased 1.66-fold (exact interaction P = 0.09; q = 0.22). In UK2035, the combination increased the labeled IMP/(ATP+GTP+UTP) ratio 3.64-fold (model interaction P = 3.2 x 10-4; exact P = 0.016; q = 0.097). No endpoint survived Benjamini-Hochberg correction at q < 0.05 in the exact analyses. The reanalysis reproduced the direction of the source study's principal labeling patterns but showed that their statistical support is weaker than model-based P values imply.
